messages.subject: add unseen animals to capthist
messages.body_plain:
Hello, I am new to secr and running mark-resight models.  I have multiple sessions where some animals are marked and seen on camera, some animals are marked and not seen on camera, and some animals seen on camera are not marked.  The marking process takes place outside of the camera session and is opportunistic hunter trapping-so would be difficult to model.

So I have managed to get secr to run multisession data for sessions where I have marked animals that are seen.  BUT when I try to include include a session where there were no marked animals seen on camera like this........

Session Animal Occasion Trap
S2         NONE        0               0

I get an error regarding missing or duplicated animal names and no live releases for S2. Even if I put the phrase nocapt="NONE" in the call to read.capthist
Ideally I would like to get the known marked animals in caphist even if they were not captured because I do have telemetry data on these animals that I would like to use to estimate sigma.

I have tried the following to no avail, I get errors that the trap location doesn't match anything in the trap file - which it doesn't of course.  But I'm not sure how to format these guys that I know were marked and in the area but were never seen.

S3  ABC   0    0
S3  XYZ  0   0

Thanks,

Robin

messages.subject: Re: add unseen animals to capthist
messages.body_plain:
Robin
I personally have two problems with this
1. Mark-resight analyses tend to be flimsy and unconvincing because of errors in recording marks and mark status, doubtful independence of repeat sightings etc. The problems are magnified when you can't model the marking process, as the spatial distribution of marked animals is then pretty much a guess. The problems are not solved by bringing in telemetry data: this may or may not be representative, and with rare exceptions helps only to pin down the sigma parameter. Spatial mark-resight may work with careful design and large samples, but both are rare. This is my personal take, and you didn't ask for that, but it explains why I limit my support: it's up to others who are more enthusiastic to weigh in.
2. I can't put my finger on your data issue. It is possible that 'secr' does not handle multi-session mark-resight analyses with no marked animals in some sessions - I would have to check. That would be easier if we had a minimal example, including a dataset and R code. Can you provide (offline if necessary)?
Murray

messages.subject: Re: Raster errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray,
Thanks for the response.
tmask is the mask made from the traps object in my data. The warning appears regardless of whether i include the mask in the predictDsurface function or not, so I don't think it's that particular object but it sounds like it's definitely related to the trap layout. But for reference, here's what's creating the tmask object:
> tmask = make.mask(traps(woylie.cap),spacing=50, buffer = 600, type = 'trapbuffer')

summary(tmask[[2]]) looks exactly how i would expect it to.

After having a play around with the raster creation, including digging into the source code for the function, i think it's due to my trap layout (and as you say, therefore the mask) being non uniform across the study area and that is throwing off the step in the raster creation when the function tries to create a matrix from the extracted Dsurface data.

Given that it seems to be my trap layout that's the problem, i have come up with the following workaround which gets me the raster i'm after (but it's probably not the most elegant solution). There may be better ways to go about this?

########################################
surf = Dsurf[[2]] # Get a Dsurface from particular session

# Extract relevant data from the Dsurface object
ras.data = data.frame(x=surf[,1],
                        y=surf[,2],
                        D.0 = covariates(surf)[,1])

ggplot(ras.data) + geom_tile(aes(x=x,y=y, fill=D.0)) # Check that the density data looks right when plotted

# Create the raster from the data
ras = raster::rasterFromXYZ(ras.data, res=spacing(surf), crs=sp::CRS("+init=epsg:32750"))
########################################

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I’m very new to capture-recapture models in general and
seeking advice from those of you with more experience.

We are monitoring cave roosting bats. We want to develop a
sampling strategy and analysis framework suitable to calculate population size
(or density If spatial models are suitable) as well as survival to monitor
population trends in the long term.

Pilot data: Individuals have been identified from
genetic profiles amplified from scat material collected under roosting sites (detectors).
The pilot data was not collected with capture-recapture analysis in mind; however,
important insights can be derived. As mentioned above, we are looking at
implementing a better sampling strategy.

Inter-annual data: Across a
four-year period 319 unique individuals have been identified and 51 individuals
have been recaptured at least once across the four years.  Of these,
35% (18 ind)  were recaptured in the same
roost, 37% (19 ind) recaptured in 2 different roosts and the remaining
individuals were detected  in 3 to 5 roosts.

Intra-annual data: when
looking at each year independently, between 56-100% of recaptures occur in the
same roost.

Given the above background here are my questions:

1.)
Would a spatial method be suitable for my
species? My initial thought was that they were not, because the great majority
of recaptures occur in the same roost and according to the secr manual, spatial
recaptures are required to derive a good estimate of D.  However, on a phidot
post <http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=34&t=3926&p=12990&hilit=Missing+occasions+on+per+individual+basis#p12990> on another animal and extreme site fidelity, it was mentioned that setting
sigma to an arbitrary number could work but caution was warranted.

Any additional thoughts? I’m thinking of
going the non-spatial route.

 2.)
What about the inter-annual data? There are
almost equal proportions of recaptures in a single or multiple roost. Would a
spatial method be advisable?  Any warnings?

 3.)
My final question is regarding the number of recaptures.
It has been mentioned that a minimum of 10-20 recaptures are required to obtain
sensible results.  Do these numbers
translate to a proportion of the captures? Or is it 20 individuals independently
of whether you capture 500 or 50 indv.

Thanks heaps,

Diana

messages.body_plain:
Hello Diana

I'm not sure I can help much. The spatial capture-recapture (SECR) models in the R package 'secr' apply to populations distributed more or less evenly in 2 dimensions. If your bats are clustered at a few roosts then that is not what you need. What density would you be estimating? The openCR phidot post (interesting - I had forgotten that!) was an attempt to deal with sporadic tree-specific sampling effort for a frog that (effectively) didn't move between trees, whereas your bats do move between roosts.

A non-spatial multi-state model for the discrete subpopulations is more suitable (e.g., Lebreton et al. 2009 Advances in Ecological Research 41). I'm not saying that is going to be easy, and you could just choose to ignore the spatial (roost) structure in a non-spatial analysis. You should find help on phidot from people who know MARK or E-SURGE.  If you estimate population size from a non-spatial model then do think about exactly what population you are trying to estimate (in spatial sampling N is usually not well defined).

One danger of ignoring spatial structure is that you miss the spatial component of individual heterogeneity in detection probability, and that can bias estimates of population size and survival. Whether that is an issue depends on other details like the ranging behaviour of the bats, the extent of the sampling are, the sampling protocols etc.

On your last question - yes, the 20 recaptures rule of thumb is independent of the total.

That's how it looks to me today - I hope you can elicit other opinions. Clustering is not uncommon, but usually it is seen just as a threat to variance estimates in SECR models, whereas in your case it is fundamental to the population structure and sampling.

Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hello Valentina
The package 'openCR' offers a method 'classMembership' for completely unknown latent classes, but openCR.fit() does not allow partially known classes (hcov). What you need is the 'secr' version of classMembership, but unfortunately it doesn't exist. It's simple enough in principle (just capture the individual likelihood components given membership in each class and see which is bigger), but because 'secr' has many options there is quite a lot of coding involved and it won't happen soon.
Murray
